title: Turkey, drumstick, cooked, skin not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Turkey is a large bird native to North America. The drumstick is one of the most meaty parts, low in fat. When boiled without the skin, it retains protein and essential micronutrients while keeping calories low.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turkey meat is rich in tryptophan, an amino acid that supports serotonin production.
In the United States, turkey is strongly associated with Thanksgiving celebrations.
Drumsticks contain more iron than breast meat because of their denser muscle fibers.
Compared with chicken, turkey has a more pronounced flavor, making it popular in Asian cuisines.
The skin of turkey holds most of the fat, so it is often removed to reduce caloric content.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: A 100‑g serving of cooked, skin‑less drumstick provides about 29 g of high‑quality protein, essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: Without skin, the fat content is under 2 g per 100 g, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Turkey supplies vitamin B6, niacin (B3) and riboflavin (B2), which support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: The drumstick provides iron, zinc and phosphorus, important for blood formation, immunity and bone health.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: The high protein level helps maintain a feeling of fullness, beneficial for weight management.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked turkey may harbor pathogens such as Salmonella or Campylobacter. Proper cooking temperatures are essential.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals are allergic to bird proteins, which can cause reactions ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Turkey is relatively high in purines, so people with gout should limit intake.

items.title: Sodium in processed versions
items.content: If the drumstick has been brined or marinated, sodium levels can be high, which is a concern for hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked, skin‑less drumstick can be diced for salads, added to soups and stews, or used in sandwiches. After boiling, a quick sauté gives a pleasant golden crust.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked turkey in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in sealed bags for 2‑3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 74 °C before serving.
